prompt:
A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world each placement lands at the left-right mirror of the chosen anchor: a brick dx cells wide chosen at column x lands at column 8 - dx - x, in the same row. The valid-action mask is in the agent's own action terms. The designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
No trials yet. The starting network learned to press DONE straight away: 100% DONE, with episode length already 1.6 at 25% of training. In this world each placement lands at the left-right mirror of the chosen anchor. The starting head scores each anchor from features at that anchor, but the brick fills cells at the mirrored columns. So almost every placement in the early sampled actions put cells outside the target and earned negative reward, and DONE at 0 was the best option. The structural fix is to give the head feature maps aligned with where the brick actually lands. Flipping a learned feature map along x lines it up exactly: pooling the flipped map over the footprint at anchor x covers columns 8-dx-x to 7-x. I also compare this with a generic learned column/row mixing layer that could discover the remapping itself. Separately, the default recipe gives only about 32 updates, which is few, so one candidate tests more updates.

### Round 2
The mirror is the main obstacle. Concatenating flip_x of the trunk features into the footprint-pooling head took dev success from 0 to 0.53. Learned X-by-X and Y-by-Y remapping layers did not find the mirror in time (0.009). The recipe mattered almost as much as the head: about 83 smaller updates instead of 32 raised dev success to 0.89. The two seeds were close (0.91 and 0.87), and training success was still rising at the end (0.72 at 75%, 0.88 at 100%), so the agent is not converged yet. Dev IoU is 0.984 with only 0.42 cells outside the target per episode. The remaining failures are therefore probably rare ordering or sealing mistakes, whose cost only shows several steps later. This round tests three refinements of the best trial (r1c2), one change each: (1) even more updates and samples, (2) a longer credit horizon for delayed sealing errors, (3) local spatial context in the head, in the action frame.

### Round 3
Results so far:
- **Mirror alignment is what made learning possible.** Feeding the head flip_x(f) took dev success from 0 to 0.53 with the default recipe.
- **About 77 updates of 2048 samples (r1c2) gave 0.89, with both seeds steady.** Raising gamma to 0.99 changed nothing (0.876).
- **Spending more compute per sample hurt.** The 3x3 projection cost 1.5x the FLOPs, so it trained on about 30% fewer samples, and it dropped to 0.65. This suggests the task is limited by samples.
- **r2c1 collapsed to DONE on both seeds.** It used a 1024-sample batch and 2 epochs. Both runs took about the same number of gradient steps, so the cause is either the smaller batch or the fewer epochs per update. Next round separates these.
- **Learning the remapping from scratch failed** (r1c3, generic x and y mixing).

Training success was still rising at the end (0.72 to 0.88), and dev IoU is 0.98, so the remaining failures look like ordering mistakes that more samples should fix. A collapse to DONE is the main risk when the best trial is retrained on 4 new seeds.

### Round 4
Mirroring the trunk features to match the hidden landing rule is what makes learning work. Without it the agent collapses to DONE. With the default recipe it reaches 0.53, and with more, smaller updates (128 envs, 3 epochs) about 0.88–0.89. Doubling lr to 0.002 gave the best result so far, 0.93, with both seeds at 0.93. The other changes landed within noise of 0.89: longer horizon (0.876), 2 epochs (0.886) and a four-view flip bank (0.90). A 3x3 head projection did worse (0.65) because it is costly and gets fewer samples. Learned remapping (r1c3) and very small batches (r2c1) failed. Dev IoU is about 0.99, so the remaining failures are mostly overhang and ordering errors. One trace has matching column heights but the wrong cells filled. This is the last round, so I will refine the r3c2 recipe, which has the best evidence behind it, with one change per candidate: a higher lr, more samples, or less entropy for sharper greedy policies.

## Trial it ended with
name: mirror head, lr 0.002
hypothesis: Same as r1c2 but with the learning rate doubled to 0.002, still decaying linearly to 0. Training success was still rising at the end, so learning seems limited by how fast the policy improves per update, and a larger step should get further on the same 158k samples. Refuted if the 2-seed mean is at or below 0.87, or if a seed becomes unstable or collapses to DONE. That would mean step size is not the bottleneck.

Return a JSON object: "verdict" ("yes", "partly" or "no") and "evidence" (at most 80 words, quoting the text and
naming the round it comes from).
